author: kijakubovs86334
text:
🚨 I'M 18. I BUILT A GTA-STYLE BROWSER GAME FOR $20 — AGENCIES SELL THIS FOR $5,000 🎮

It took 10 minutes. One prompt. One Claude tab. No engine. No artist. No team.

Pause at 0:05. Look at the HUD.

"Driving" mode. Wanted stars. Cash counter. Weapon slot. Radar in the bottom left. On-screen controls in the bottom right.

That is a full game loop. Cars, pedestrians, money, police, weapons, missions. Running in a browser. No download.

I opened Claude and typed seven sentences:

→ small low-poly city with houses, roads, and trees
→ a player car with chase camera and acceleration
→ police that spawn when you commit a crime
→ a wanted level system with stars
→ a pistol the player can fire on foot
→ a money counter and a radar in the corner
→ basic missions and a scoreboard

It returned a playable prototype. In the browser. In ten minutes.

The economy I just walked into:

→ Agencies charge brands $3,000–$5,000 for one branded mini-game
→ Studio version: 1 developer, 1 designer, 1 artist, 3 weeks of revisions
→ My version: a $20 Claude subscription and a kitchen table
→ The client cannot tell the difference, because the client wanted shares, not photorealism

This is not GTA 6. It was never supposed to be.

Brands do not need GTA 6. They need something a person clicks, plays, sends to a friend, and remembers longer than a banner ad.

Here's what nobody is talking about:

The skill is no longer building the game. The skill is knowing which "$5,000 agency products" were already secretly $20 of compute and a teenager with taste.

Most people are still arguing whether AI can replace developers.

Meanwhile, I closed two demos before lunch.

The easiest money window is not "learning to code faster." It is selling what people still think takes a full team.

Bookmark this.

The race for cheap creative just left the studio.

Literally.
